The Fork-tailed woodnymph (Thalurania furcata) is a hummingbird species distributed across much of the Amazon basin and the Guiana Shield. Field studies of its reproductive biology indicate that females construct a small cup nest and lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a value consistent with the modal clutch size observed across the Trochilidae. Observations of marked individuals further suggest that a typical breeding season may include two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually]. Developing embryos within eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require approximately 16.5 days [ab = approximately 16.5 days] to complete their development and hatch, which is a duration well within the range reported for other medium-sized hummingbirds. The newly hatched nestling, entirely dependent on parental provisioning, emerges at a remarkably small mass. Hatchlings weigh only about 0.5 grams [Ww0 = about 0.5 grams] immediately after emerging from the egg, representing an extremely altricial state typical of the family. This initial mass is a fraction of what the individual will eventually attain as a fully grown adult.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a pattern common among hummingbirds. Sexually mature females reach a maximum reported body mass of 4.2 grams [Wwi = 4.2 grams], whereas adult males, which are typically larger, attain an asymptotic mass of approximately 4.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 4.9 grams]. This difference is reflected in the species' ecology, as males are often more aggressive in defending floral territories. The growth trajectory from the 0.5 gram hatchling to these adult masses is rapid, fueled by a diet of nectar and small arthropods. Under the thermal conditions associated with active daily metabolism in this tropical species, roughly 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the nestling phase progresses quickly. Fledging, defined as the achievement of first sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is typical for hummingbirds and reflects a strategy of high parental investment to produce a mobile juvenile capable of independent foraging.

Puberty and the onset of reproductive capability in the Fork-tailed woodnymph occur some time after fledging. Under the typical thermal regime of active foraging, recorded as 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], young birds reach sexual maturity at 57 days after hatching [tp = 57 days after hatching]. This relatively quick attainment of maturity means that individuals born early in the breeding season can potentially reproduce within the same year. The first successful breeding event, however, is often deferred beyond the point of mere physiological readiness. Longevity data for the Fork-tailed woodnymph are limited, but extrapolations based on the closely related and well-studied Black-chinned Hummingbird (Archilochus alexandri) provide a useful benchmark. Under the sustained thermal conditions of an active metabolism, estimated at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the maximum lifespan is projected to be approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This figure is consistent with the known longevity of several other small Neotropical hummingbird species and suggests a life-history strategy that balances a rapid early development and high annual reproductive output against a moderate to long adult lifespan. The maximum daily reproductive rate, calculated from the clutch size of two eggs and the potential for two clutches per year, yields an annual output of four eggs per female. When evaluated at the active metabolic temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], this rate of 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch] with 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year] is typical for a hummingbird of this body size and is likely constrained by the high energetic cost of egg production and the intensive parental care required by altricial young.

The Fork-tailed woodnymph occupies a specialized niche as a traplining pollinator, visiting a variety of understory and canopy flowers. This foraging strategy is energetically demanding, and the species shows a high mass-specific metabolic rate. The 0.5 gram hatchling must transition through a series of developmental stages, each with its own energetic requirements.
